abstract: Understanding the drivers of bee phenology is important for predicting how climate change may alter the temporal overlap between bee activity and plant flowering, with consequences for pollination. We documented unusually early emergence of Melissodes tepidus timberlakei Cockerell, 1926 at a perennial nesting site in spring 2026 and examined the relationship between emergence and climatic conditions with (1) five years of nesting observations at a single site, and (2) 119 years of M. tepidus occurrence records from across the western United States. We found that warming temperatures were associated with earlier emergence, whereas precipitation was not, and we emphasize the utility of monitoring ground nests to understand emergence drivers in bees during ongoing climate change.
